questions.question: What balance do I use to calculate my 2026 RMD?
questions.answer: Generally use the eligible account balance on December 31, 2025, with any required adjustments confirmed by the custodian. A current balance after market moves is not the ordinary calculation base.

questions.question: Which age determines the RMD factor?
questions.answer: Use the age you reach by the end of the distribution year. Table II requires both spouses’ ages when its younger sole-beneficiary spouse conditions apply.

questions.question: Does withholding count toward the amount withdrawn?
questions.answer: Use the gross eligible distribution credited by the custodian, including amounts withheld for tax. The net deposit into your bank account is not necessarily the RMD credit.

questions.question: Can I carry an excess withdrawal forward to next year?
questions.answer: No. Taking more than one year’s RMD does not create credit against a later year’s requirement. The next calculation uses its own balance, age and rules.

questions.question: Can I calculate an inherited IRA RMD with this tool?
questions.answer: No. This model is for supported owner accounts. Beneficiary status, inheritance date, owner death and other conditions affect inherited-account rules; use appropriate IRS guidance and custodian advice.

questions.question: Does dividing the RMD by twelve create a monthly deadline?
questions.answer: No. It is a budgeting equivalent. Confirm the annual deadline and your custodian’s processing schedule; the tool does not mandate monthly distributions.

limitations: Owner-account illustration using verified post-2021 tables; no inherited-account, still-working exception or individualized deadline determination.
Gross RMD is not take-home income. Withholding, marginal tax brackets and Medicare-related effects are not calculated.
Future returns and year-end withdrawal timing are projection assumptions, not IRS-mandated account performance.

meta.title: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.heading: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.description: Calculate two-tier 401(k) matching, distinguish match rate from salary band, and understand contribution limits, payroll timing, true-ups and vesting.
meta.breadcrumb: How Does 401(k) Matching Work? Formulas and Checked Examples
meta.cardIntro: Calculate two-tier 401(k) matching, distinguish match rate from salary band, and understand contribution limits, payroll timing, true-ups and vesting.

matching.intro: A 401(k) employer match adds money under your employer’s plan formula when you make qualifying contributions. The match rate tells you how much the employer adds per eligible dollar. The contribution band tells you how much of your pay is eligible for that rate. Read both numbers together; a 50% match does not usually mean the employer deposits half of your annual salary.
matching.answer: At $80,000 annual salary, a plan matching 100% of the first 3% contributed plus 50% of the next 2% requires a $4,000 employee contribution to capture the full modeled match. The employer contributes $3,200, or 4% of salary. The combined $7,200 contribution is not the same as contributing only 4% yourself.

sections.title: Translate the match sentence into contribution bands
paragraphs: Break the formula into separate slices. The first 3% of $80,000 is $2,400, matched dollar for dollar. The next 2% is $1,600, matched at 50% for another $800. Adding the two employer amounts gives $3,200. Employee contributions across both bands total $4,000, or 5% of salary.

In the calculator’s second tier, enter the additional band, not the cumulative threshold. For “100% on the first 3%, then 50% through 5%,” the additional second band is 2%, not 5%. A wrong interpretation would model an 8% combined band and overstate the employee contribution needed.
sections.formula: Employer match = eligible first-band employee dollars × first rate + eligible additional-band dollars × second rate

sections.title: Same salary, three matching policies
paragraphs: Our chart holds salary at $80,000 and assumes the employee contributes enough to earn the full modeled match. The two-tier example produces $3,200. A 50% match on the first 6% needs $4,800 employee dollars and produces $2,400 employer dollars. A 100% match on the first 6% also needs $4,800 but produces $4,800.

These controlled hypothetical policies demonstrate why headline match percentages are insufficient for comparing benefits. They are not a survey of typical employers. Compare eligibility, vesting, eligible compensation, contribution timing and other benefits before deciding which employment package is better.

sections.title: Employee deferrals and employer additions have different limits
paragraphs: For 2026, the basic employee elective-deferral limit is $24,500. Eligible participants age 50 or older may have an $8,000 catch-up, with the higher $11,250 catch-up applying at ages 60 through 63 if permitted. These are limits, not automatic entitlements to employer matching. Use calendar-year-end age and check plan eligibility.

The model uses the 2026 $360,000 eligible-compensation cap and $72,000 annual-additions cap excluding employee catch-up. Employer matching does not consume the employee elective-deferral limit, but combined additions have their own constraints. Other plans, prior contributions and plan restrictions can require adjustments outside this simplified full-year model.

In the high-salary case, $400,000 salary does not make all pay match-eligible: compensation is capped at $360,000. A 100% match on the first 10% would require $36,000 employee contributions. A 35-year-old’s $24,500 deferral limit prevents that under our assumptions, so the tool reports a partial match and explicitly labels full matching unattainable.

sections.title: Why reaching the limit early can change the match
paragraphs: The Maximize Employer Match mode assumes equal pay, a constant contribution percentage, per-pay-period matching and no annual true-up. The upper steady rate spreads the age-based employee limit over annual salary. If contributions stop before year-end, later pay periods may have no employee deferral to match.

Some plans reconcile matching annually through a true-up; others do not, and conditions can vary. Bonuses, pay changes, midyear enrollment and prior year-to-date contributions also change the payroll problem. Ask the administrator how your actual plan treats them. The calculator’s steady-rate window is not a personalized payroll election.

sections.title: A credited match is different from money you are entitled to keep
paragraphs: Employee contributions and their earnings are fully vested, while employer contributions may be subject to a vesting schedule depending on plan design. The calculator reports modeled employer deposits without applying a vesting haircut. A $3,200 match is therefore not a guarantee that a departing employee keeps all $3,200.

Read the summary plan description for match formula, eligible pay, vesting, timing and true-up provisions. For a long-term projection, use the tool’s separate projection mode and review its contribution timing and fixed-year limits. A yearly matching calculation alone says nothing about future investment returns, tax treatment at withdrawal or how long savings will last.

questions.question: What does a 50% 401(k) match up to 6% mean?
questions.answer: Under that formula, each qualifying employee dollar receives 50 cents from the employer, up to employee contributions equal to 6% of eligible pay. At $80,000, $4,800 employee contributions can earn $2,400 employer contributions before other applicable restrictions.

questions.question: Does my employer match count toward the $24,500 employee limit?
questions.answer: Employer matching does not use the 2026 employee elective-deferral limit. Combined employee and employer annual additions have a separate limit, and catch-up contributions have separate treatment.

questions.question: How do I enter a two-tier matching formula?
questions.answer: Enter the first band and match rate, then the additional second band and its rate. A formula running from 3% through 5% has a 2% second band, not 5%.

questions.question: Should I contribute the annual maximum as early as possible?
questions.answer: That depends on the plan’s matching timing and true-up provisions. With per-pay-period matching and no true-up, stopping deferrals early may lose later matching opportunities. This mode illustrates a steady full-year rate rather than optimizing every payroll.

questions.question: Is the employer match immediately vested?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. The plan’s vesting rules govern ownership of employer contributions. This calculator reports the modeled deposit and does not calculate a forfeiture at departure.

questions.question: Can this mode calculate a midyear payroll change?
questions.answer: Not directly. It assumes full-year employment, equal pay, constant contributions and no prior year-to-date deferrals. Use your actual payroll and plan information for a midyear election.

limitations: Matching rules are hypothetical inputs. This guide does not assert that a particular employer offers them or that every plan permits catch-up contributions.
The steady-rate model excludes bonuses, unequal pay, prior contributions, annual true-ups and vesting adjustments.
2026 contribution limits are versioned inputs, not a forecast of later years or a guarantee that payroll accepts the displayed rate.
